title: 29 U.S.C. § 1001 — Congressional Findings and Declaration of Policy (ERISA § 2)
built_by: Claude (assistant) under direction of Michael Hartmann
note_on_type: § 1001 is a congressional findings provision, not an operative cause of action. Its role in the corpus is interpretive: courts use it as the 'thumb on the scale' for construing ambiguous ERISA provisions in favor of participants. It is built here because it is the wound-and-promise statement for all of ERISA, and every other standard in this Citizen inherits from it.

evolution_stages.key_change: Congressional findings enacted; § 1001(b) four-part policy declaration; § 1001(c) vesting/funding/PBGC mandate
Text unchanged since 1974; pointer to current/

case_law.case: Massachusetts Mutual Life Ins. Co. v. Russell
case_law.rule: Courts should interpret ERISA to further its protective purpose as stated in § 1001; breach of fiduciary duty under § 1109 does not support extracontractual compensatory damages for individual beneficiary — the remedy runs to the plan; confirmed ERISA's make-whole-the-plan (not the individual) structure

interpretive_use: In any ERISA argument where a provision is ambiguous or where the defendant invokes a restrictive reading, cite § 1001(b) and (c) for the proposition that Congress intended to protect participants and to ensure ready access to federal courts. Courts applying Firestone, Amara, and other foundational cases routinely begin with § 1001 as the statement of ERISA's core purpose.
